analysis.one_liner: Requires the Supreme Court and other federal judges to adopt enforceable ethics and recusal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it received no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Supreme Court and lower federal courts to issue formal codes of conduct for judges, with public notice and comment. It would set minimum disclosure rules for gifts, travel, and income received by justices and their law clerks, expand the circumstances requiring a judge to step aside from a case — including when a party helped fund the judge's appointment or paid the judge within the past six years — and create a process for parties to challenge a judge's refusal to step aside before a panel of outside judges. It would also require parties and groups filing friend-of-the-court briefs to disclose money they or their lawyers gave to justices.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who appear before federal courts as parties, defendants, or members of the public affected by court rulings. The bill would give them a enforceable way to know when a judge has financial ties to the other side, and a formal process — a motion reviewed by a panel of outside judges — to challenge a judge who stays on a case despite a conflict. Currently, Supreme Court justices answer to no binding ethics code and decide recusal questions themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Litigants and the public relying on impartial courts

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for its justices and staff, with public notice and comment, within 180 days of enactment.
Requires justices and their law clerks to disclose gifts, travel, and income at least at the level members of Congress must disclose.

Expands mandatory disqualification to cases where a party or its affiliate lobbied for or spent substantial money supporting the judge's nomination or appointment, or paid the judge, the judge's spouse, or their businesses within six years of the case.

Creates a formal disqualification process: a party can file a motion with an affidavit, the judge must either step aside or send the question to a randomly selected panel of outside judges, and the case is stayed until it is resolved.

Requires parties and amicus groups to disclose in their briefs any gifts, income, or reimbursements their side, their lawyers, or their officers gave to a justice during the case, plus any spending supporting the justice's appointment.

Requires public posting on court websites of every disqualification, with an explanation of the reasons, and directs the Federal Judicial Center to study compliance with recusal rules every two years.

analysis.who_pays: Judges and justices, who would lose the ability to decide their own conflicts and would face mandatory disclosure of gifts, travel, and income. Law firms and interest groups that use amicus briefs would have to disclose funding behind them, and parties would face added paperwork. Some disqualification motions could add delay to cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Justices, judges, and the lawyers arguing before them

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves one self-review problem intact: the Supreme Court itself would be the reviewing panel for a motion to disqualify a justice, so other justices would still judge a colleague's conflicts.
Gift, travel, and income disclosure rules for justices would be written by the Court's own Counselor with the Chief Justice's approval, keeping part of the system in the Court's own hands.

The mandatory recusal triggers are broad — any payment from a party or affiliate within six years, regardless of size or relevance — which could sweep in routine connections and generate disqualification motions that delay proceedings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: the Supreme Court is the only major American court with no binding code of conduct, and justices decide their own recusal, so financial conflicts visible to the public at other courts have gone undisclosed. The bill addresses that with disclosure, expanded recusal grounds, and an outside review process. The costs are mostly administrative, though the six-year lookback recusal rule is drawn broadly enough to invite delay tactics, and the bill preserves two openings for the Court to keep judging itself. On balance a strong integrity bill with some design rough edges.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held it or brought it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on May 11, 2022, joined by six original Senate cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill drew 15 cosponsors — 14 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Senate Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting justices and judges keep the existing arrangement, in which the Supreme Court has no binding ethics code and judges decide their own conflicts. Interest groups and law firms that fund friend-of-the-court campaigns also avoid new disclosure requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal judges and justices keeping self-policing

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court ethics and recusal bill and assembled original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independents; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Supreme Court justices and the federal judiciary
industries.note: The bill ends judicial self-policing: binding codes of conduct, mandatory gift and income disclosure, expanded recusal grounds, and outside review of disqualification disputes. Judges and justices would bear the compliance burden and lose discretion over their own conflicts.

industries.industry: Law firms and litigants in the Supreme Court bar
industries.note: Parties and their lawyers would have to disclose in filings any money they gave to justices during a case, and courts could strike amicus briefs that would create a disqualifying conflict. This raises the visibility — and the risk — of the financial machinery behind Supreme Court advocacy.

industries.industry: Interest groups funding amicus brief campaigns
industries.note: Any organization filing a friend-of-the-court brief must disclose contributors who gave 3% of its revenue or more than $100,000 in the prior year, with an annual government audit. Groups that preferred not to reveal who bankrolls their briefs lose that discretion.
